Probing Quantum Spin Systems with Kolmogorov-Arnold Neural Network Quantum States

Mahmud Ashraf Shamim Email: mashamim@crimson.ua.edu Affiliation: Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, 35487, Alabama, USA.    Eric A. F. Reinhardt Email: eareinhardt@crimson.ua.edu Affiliation: Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, 35487, Alabama, USA.    Talal Ahmed Chowdhury Email: talal@ku.edu Affiliation: Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Kansas, Lawrence, Kansas 66045, USA. Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Dhaka, P.O. Box 1000, Dhaka, Bangladesh.    Sergei Gleyzer Affiliation: Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, 35487, Alabama, USA.    Paulo T Araujo Affiliation: Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, 35487, Alabama, USA.
Abstract

Neural Quantum States (NQS) are a class of variational wave functions parametrized by neural networks (NNs) to study quantum many-body systems. In this work, we propose SineKAN, a NQS ansatz based on Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs), to represent quantum mechanical wave functions as nested univariate functions. We show that SineKAN wavefunction with learnable sinusoidal activation functions can capture the ground state energies, fidelities and various correlation functions of the one dimensional Transverse-Field Ising model, Anisotropic Heisenberg model, and Antiferromagnetic J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model with different chain lengths. In our study of the J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model with L=100L=100 sites, we find that the SineKAN model outperforms several previously explored neural quantum state ansätze, including Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs), Long Short-Term Memory models (LSTMs), and Multi-layer Perceptrons (MLP) a.k.a. Feed Forward Neural Networks, when compared to the results obtained from the Density Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG) algorithm. We find that SineKAN models can be trained to high precisions and accuracies with minimal computational costs.

I Introduction

Understanding the properties of strongly correlated many-body quantum systems is a major challenge in modern physics. This challenge arises from the complexity of many-body interactions and the exponential growth of the Hilbert space, making exact encoding of the ground state (GS) wave function nearly impossible. Variational methods provide an effective approach to tackle this problem by employing parameterized trial wave functions and minimizing their energy expectation values, thereby enabling an efficient representation of quantum states [1, 2].

Recently, in a seminal work, Carleo and Troyer [3] introduced a variational ansatz in which a neural network (NN) parametrizes the many-body wave-function. This approach, known as the NN quantum state (NQS), leverages quantum Monte Carlo methods [2] and the expressive power of NNs [4] to capture complex quantum correlations. This work shows that shallow networks, such as restricted Boltzmann machines (RBM), can efficiently approximate the GSs of the quantum Ising and antiferromagnetic Heisenberg models, and are also able to capture volume-law entanglement entropy [5], opening a new avenue for representing variational wave functions.

As a subsequent development, various NQS architectures, such as Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) [6, 7, 8, 9], Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) [10, 11, 12, 13], Autoregressive Models [14, 15], and Vision Transformers (ViTs) [16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22], have been proposed, each with varying degrees of effectiveness and expressibility, along with hybrid approaches that combine traditional variational wave functions and NNs [23, 24]. For a recent discussion and review of the expressibility of the NQS, please see Refs. [25, 26].

NQSs are generally based on architectures involving feature extraction followed by Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) [27]. These classic MLPs are feedforward neural networks with nonlinear activation functions.

In a recent work, Liu et al. introduced Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) [28], offering a promising alternative to traditional MLPs. These networks are motivated by the Kolmogorov-Arnold superposition theorem (KAST) that states that any continuous multivariate function can be represented by a two-layer model composed of univariate functions [29, 30]. The original work explored the use of basis-splines as the learnable, on-edge function. However, a broad class of basis functions are possible, which has motivated the exploration of different KAN architectures beyond the original basis-spline ansatz [28]. Such work has included rational functions [31], radial basis functions [32], wavelet functions [33], Jacobi basis functions [34], Chebyshev polynomials [35] and sinusoidal basis functions [36]. Numerous follow-up works have shown the viability to various degrees of different KAN architectures across a broad range of tasks [37].

In this paper, we explore a new class of NQS architecture that utilizes a KAN with sinusoidal activation functions, called the SineKAN ansatz (see fig. 1). SineKAN [36] has already demonstrated superior performance in various tasks compared to other KAN architectures, such as image classification, in terms of numerical accuracy and computational efficiency. The primary motivation for selecting SineKAN as a variational wave function lies in its periodic and smoothly differentiable functional form, which makes it an effective approximator for a variety of functions. We benchmark the SineKAN ansatz by computing the GS energies, fidelity and various correlation functions of the 1D transverse field Ising model (TFIM), anisotropic Heisenberg model (AHM) [38], and antiferromagnetic Heisenberg J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model. In each model for different chain lengths, we find excellent agreement in GS energies and correlation functions determined by Exact Diagonalization (ED) and the state-of-the-art Density Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG) methods, and SineKAN which required only a modest number of variational parameters.

The paper is organized as follows. In section II, we introduce the Kolmogorov Arnold variational wave function and discuss different models we use for benchmarking our architectures in section III. The Hamiltonians we study are discussed in section IV. In Section V we discuss the training methods and the hyperparameters for different Hamiltonians. In section VII, we present the results of our simulations. Section VIII is dedicated to the Marshall Sign Rule (MSR) for SineKAN, and in section IX, we discuss comparative runtime of our model with different models. Section X provides a discussion of the findings, and section XI concludes the paper with a summary and an outlook on future research directions.

II Kolmogorov-Arnold Variational Wavefunction

For a quantum mechanical system with LL sites, where each site is occupied by a single spin-12\frac{1}{2}, the dimension of the local Hilbert space is two, corresponding to the two possible spin states. In the computational basis, the spin configuration of the system is represented as σ={σ1,σ2,⋯,σL}\sigma=\{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\cdots,\sigma_{L}\}, where each σi\sigma_{i} can take the values ↑\uparrow or ↓\downarrow. A pure quantum state in this Hilbert space is a vector that can be expressed in terms of the basis states |σ⟩\ket{\sigma} as

Ψ=∑σψσ​|σ⟩\Psi=\sum_{\sigma}\psi_{\sigma}\ket{\sigma} (1)

where ψσ\psi_{\sigma} are the probability amplitudes associated to |σ⟩\ket{\sigma}.

KAST states that any multivariate continuous functional mapping can be represented by sums of univariate functions of one variable [29, 30]. As the wave functions are continuous, we can generalize this to the problem of mapping spin lattices to an associated wave function as:

Ψ≡ΨKA=∑q=12​L+1Φq​(∑p=1Lϕq,p​(σp))\Psi\equiv\Psi_{\mathrm{KA}}=\sum_{q=1}^{2L+1}\Phi_{q}\left(\sum_{p=1}^{L}\phi_{q,p}(\sigma_{p})\right) (2)

where the inner function ϕq,p:{0,1}L→ℝ\phi_{q,p}:\{0,1\}^{L}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} and the outer function Φq:ℝ→ℝ\Phi_{q}:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}, and σp\sigma_{p} are the spins are adjusted to have values of either 0 or 1 [29, 30].

Although KAST guarantees the existence of the inner functions ϕ\phi and outer function Φ\Phi, it does not specify their explicit form or provide a method for determining them. The KAN model addresses this limitation by representing each univariate function with a tunable parametrization defined by a fixed number β\beta of learnable parameters per function. For input dimension LL, there are L⁡(2​L+1)L(2L+1) inner functions and 2​L+12L+1 outer functions, resulting in a total of (2​L+1)​(L+1)(2L+1)(L+1) univariate function instances [28]. Consequently, the total number of trainable parameters becomes β⁡(2​L2+3​L+1)\beta(2L^{2}+3L+1), transforming the original function space from ℝ2L\mathbb{R}^{2^{L}} to a much more compact and scalable space ℝβ⁡(2​L2+3​L+1)\mathbb{R}^{\beta(2L^{2}+3L+1)}. Assuming there exists a family of univariate functions that can achieve a good approximation with a relatively small number of parameters β≪𝒪⁡(L2)\beta\ll\mathcal{O}(L^{2}), then the total parameter space is reduced from 𝒪⁡(2L)\mathcal{O}(2^{L}) to 𝒪⁡(L2)\mathcal{O}(L^{2}). With this approximation, for a set of parameters 𝜽=(θ1,θ2,⋯,θℓ)\bm{\theta}=(\theta_{1},\theta_{2},\cdots,\theta_{\ell}) with ℓ=β⁡(2​L2+3​L+1)\ell=\beta(2L^{2}+3L+1), the exact KA wavefunction ΨKA\Psi_{\mathrm{KA}} can be approximated by a KAN representation as

ΨKA​(σ)≈ΨKAN​(σ,𝜽).\Psi_{\mathrm{KA}}(\sigma)\approx\Psi_{\mathrm{KAN}}(\sigma;\bm{\theta}). (3)

This KAN representation of the many-body wave function can effectively be treated as the variational wavefunction with optimizable parameters 𝜽\bm{\theta} and is referred to as KA neural network quantum states ansatz. Given a Hamiltonian HH that describes local interactions among the spins, and ΨKAN≡ΨKAN​(σ,𝜽)\Psi_{\texttt{KAN}}\equiv\Psi_{\mathrm{KAN}}(\sigma;\bm{\theta}) as the variational wavefunction, its ground state energy can computed by minimizing

Eθ=⟨ΨKAN|​H​|ΨKAN⟩⟨ΨKAN|ΨKAN⟩E_{\theta}=\frac{\bra{\Psi_{\texttt{KAN}}}H\ket{\Psi_{\texttt{KAN}}}}{\braket{\Psi_{\texttt{KAN}}|\Psi_{\texttt{KAN}}}} (4)

using the standard Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) protocol (Appendix A). Using this approach, the KAN parameters (θ\theta) can be approximated even when sampling only a relatively small portion of the total 2L2^{L} Hilbert space.

In our work, we use learnable sinusoid activation functions both for the inner and outer functions based on the multi-layered SineKAN architecture [36]. SineKAN was shown in [36] to exhibit properties useful for the task of representing the wavefunctions. One such property is its ability to generalize and project periodic patterns across spaces of a large domain that it hasn’t been fitted to (something highly likely to occur in probing a Hilbert space of dimension 2L2^{L}). Additionally, it is both continuous and differentiable, which could lead to improved stability in modeling continuous quantum wave functions. We show later in this work that this ansatz is empirically effective compared to other explicitly proven approximators.

The functional form of each SineKAN layer can be expressed as follows:

ym=∑l,nL,NAm​n​l​sin⁡(ωn​xl+π​nN+π​lL+δn​l)+bmy_{m}=\sum_{l,n}^{L,N}A_{mnl}\sin\left(\omega_{n}x_{l}+\frac{\pi n}{N}+\frac{\pi l}{L}+\delta_{nl}\right)+b_{m} (5)

where ll is in the input index, nn is the grid index, mm is the output index, Al​m​nA_{lmn} are amplitudes, ωn\omega_{n} are frequencies, NN is the grid size, ll is the input size, and δl​n\delta_{ln} is a small positive random perturbation along the input and grid dimensions. The frequencies, amplitudes and biases are real-valued and serve as the learnable parameters of the model (see fig. 1).

The 1D spin lattice arranged into a chain with a periodic boundary condition (PBC) is invariant under translation and reflection about any point in the chain. Using this ansatz, it’s computationally expensive to impose translational invariance, however, invariance under a single reflection about the center can be easily achieved. To preserve reflection symmetry, the ansatz becomes:

y=S⁡(σ→)+S⁡(ℛ⁡(σ→))y=S(\vec{\sigma})+S(\mathcal{R}(\vec{\sigma})) (6)

where ℛ\mathcal{R} is a reflection operator along the 1D input dimension, SS is the same multi-layer SineKAN model, and σ→\vec{\sigma} are the set of input spins with values +1+1 or −1-1. By imposing this symmetry, we can drastically reduce the total parameter space over which we need to search. To impose such a symmetry for translational invariance would scale the model size linearly with the length of the lattice. We will refer to a regular multilayer SineKAN without reflection as vSineKAN and the version with reflection symmetry as rSineKAN.

III Benchmark NQS Models

We evaluate the effectiveness of the SineKAN ansätze by benchmarking against three widely used NQS baselines: the RBM, RNN-LSTM, and MLP, as described in section VI.1.

As the original NQS proposed by Carleo and Troyer, RBM has served as a foundational benchmark in variational studies of quantum many-body systems [3, 39]. Its main advantage is that it’s high computational efficiency for small to medium-sized systems, which allows it to scale to larger systems—up to around 100 spins—with reasonable training time, especially compared to more complex architectures like RNN-LSTM. The computational complexity of RBM is more comparable to 𝒪⁡(eN)\mathcal{O}(e^{N}), so they remain highly efficient as long as the lattice size is relatively small. Structurally, the RBM consists of a visible layer representing spin configurations and a hidden layer of binary units, connected through trainable weights without intra-layer couplings ([39, 40]). Due to this bipartite structure, RBM is particularly effective in NQS applications for unfrustrated or weakly frustrated systems.

The application of RNNs to represent GS wavefunctions in quantum spin systems is well established, with several studies demonstrating their effectiveness [6, 7]. The motivation behind the choice of RNN architectures is that they generally encode some information about long-term and short-term “memory” across the length of inputs in a sequence. The idea in this case is that the memory of the models could capture short- and/or long-range dependencies across the spin lattice. Here we use a long-short-term memory (RNN-LSTM) as compared to alternative GRU or simple RNN used in [6, 7] due to previous literature findings that RNN-LSTM generally outperform the other RNN models on large datasets and sequences where very-long-term memory is not necessary [41, 42].

Finally, we compare against a MLP [27]. This architecture is nearly ubiquitous in modern machine learning. It’s commonly used following some sort of feature extractor as in the case of CNN, RNN, and Transformers. We will benchmark against two versions of MLP, one we will call vMLP which is a simple MLP with ReLU activations in hidden layers and one called rMLP which, similarly to rSineKAN, includes a second forward pass of the reflected lattice. This is a natural comparison for the SineKAN to show the advantage provided by on-edge learnable activations compared to learnable on-edge weights and fixed activations on node.

MLP ([27]) is compared pictorially in fig. 1. The main differences are the fixed learning rate (typically ReLU [43]) and that all learnable weights and biases are applied on the edge of the graph before passing through the activation function.

IV Model Hamiltonians

Our study focuses on evaluating how well the SineKAN captures the GS properties of the three different 1D quantum spin models: (1) TFIM, (2) AHM [38], and (3) antiferromagnetic J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model, all with PBC. Their Hamiltonians are given by

HTFIM=−J∑iσ^ziσ^zi+1−h∑iσ^xiH_{\mathrm{TFIM}}=-J\sum_{i}\hat{\sigma}^{z}_{i}\hat{\sigma}^{z}_{i+1}-h\sum_{i}\hat{\sigma}^{x}_{i} (7)
H^γ=∑i[(1+γ)​S^iz​S^i+1z+(1−γ)​(S^ix​S^i+1x+S^iy​S^i+1y)]\hat{H}_{\gamma}=\sum_{i}[(1+\gamma)\hat{S}^{z}_{i}\hat{S}^{z}_{i+1}+(1-\gamma)(\hat{S}^{x}_{i}\hat{S}^{x}_{i+1}+\hat{S}^{y}_{i}\hat{S}^{y}_{i+1})] (8)

and

H^J1−J2=J1​∑i𝐒^i.𝐒^i+1+J2​∑i𝐒^i.𝐒^i+2\hat{H}_{J_{1}-J_{2}}=J_{1}\sum_{i}\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{i}.\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{i+1}+J_{2}\sum_{i}\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{i}.\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{i+2} (9)

where 𝐒^i=(S^ix,S^iy,S^iz)\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{i}=(\hat{S}_{i}^{x},\hat{S}_{i}^{y},\hat{S}_{i}^{z}) are the spin-12\frac{1}{2} operators acting on site ii. The anisotropy parameter −1≤γ≤1-1\leq\gamma\leq 1, J1>0J_{1}>0 and J2≥0J_{2}\geq 0 are the nearest and next-nearest-neighbor antiferromagnetic couplings, respectively. These two models become identical when J1=1,J2=0J_{1}=1,J_{2}=0 and γ=0\gamma=0.

The TFIM describes a system of spin-12\frac{1}{2} particles arranged on a 1D lattice with interaction between nearest-neighbor spins and an external magnetic field. The coupling JJ in HTFIMH_{\mathrm{TFIM}} represents the ferromagnetic Ising interaction, which favors adjacent spins in the zz-direction. The strength of the external magnetic field is given by hh which acts along the xx-axis, inducing quantum fluctuations that compete with the ferromagnetic interaction. The σ^ix\hat{\sigma}^{x}_{i} and σ^iz\hat{\sigma}^{z}_{i} are the Pauli spin operators at the site ii. In the thermodynamic limit, this model exhibits a quantum phase transition (QPT) in a critical magnetic field hc=Jh_{c}=J separating a ferromagnetic phase (h<hch<h_{c}) and a paramagnetic phase (h>hch>h_{c}). At the critical point, the system undergoes a continuous phase transition belonging to the 2D classical Ising model class.

The Hamiltonian HγH_{\gamma} defines a 1D quantum spin-12\frac{1}{2} chain with anisotropic couplings in different spin directions. The model is an exactly solvable free‐fermion chain at γ=−1\gamma=-1, reduces to the S​U​(2)SU(2)‐invariant Heisenberg chain at γ=0\gamma=0, and in the limit γ→1\gamma\to 1 becomes the classical antiferromagnetic Ising chain in the zz-basis with two-fold degenerate Néel product-state ground states. In the thermodynamic limit the system lies in a gapless Luttinger-liquid phase with algebraic spin correlations for γ∈[−1,0]\gamma\in[-1,0], whereas for γ>0\gamma>0 it develops a finite spin gap and Néel order; these two regimes are separated by a quantum critical point at γ=0\gamma=0.

Antiferromagnetic J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} is a paradigmatic model for studying frustrated magnetism with rich GS properties. Its phase diagram is well understood through analytical and numerical methods [44, 45]. For J2=0J_{2}=0 the model becomes exactly solvable by the celebrated Bethe ansatz solution [46]. With an increasing value of J2J_{2}, it undergoes a quantum phase transition from the gapless spin-fluid phase to a spontaneously dimerized gapped valence bond state (VBS) phase. The critical value of J2J_{2} has been determined with high accuracy as J2c=0.241167±0.000005J_{2}^{c}=0.241167\pm 0.000005 [47]. The model becomes solvable at the Majumdar-Ghosh (MG) point J2=0.5J_{2}=0.5 with a two-fold degenerate VBS GS [48].

For the Hamiltonians H^γ\hat{H}_{\gamma} and H^J1−J2\hat{H}_{J_{1}-J_{2}}, when either J1=0J_{1}=0 or J2=0J_{2}=0, the spin chains are unfrustrated and bipartite, allowing a natural division into two sublattices, AA and BB. In such cases, the GS wavefunction exhibits a characteristic sign structure known as the Marshall Sign Rule (MSR) [49, 50]. Explicitly, the GS can be written as:

Ψ⁡(σ)=(−1)NA​(σ)​Ψ~​(σ),\Psi(\sigma)=(-1)^{N_{A}(\sigma)}\,\tilde{\Psi}(\sigma), (10)

where NA​(σ)=∑i∈AσiN_{A}(\sigma)=\sum_{i\in A}\sigma_{i}, with σi=0\sigma_{i}=0 or 11 encoding spin-down and spin-up respectively, and Ψ~​(σ)≥0\tilde{\Psi}(\sigma)\geq 0 is a real, non-negative amplitude in the Ising basis. This sign structure can be eliminated by a unitary transformation R^\hat{R}, defined by: R^​|σ⟩=(−1)NA​(σ)​|σ⟩\hat{R}\ket{\sigma}=(-1)^{N_{A}(\sigma)}\ket{\sigma}, which acts as a basis rotation that absorbs the alternating sign from the wavefunction into the Hamiltonian. The rotated Hamiltonian, H^rot=R^​H^​R^†\hat{H}_{\mathrm{rot}}=\hat{R}\hat{H}\hat{R}^{\dagger}, then has strictly non-positive off-diagonal elements in the Ising basis. This guarantees that the GS of H^rot\hat{H}_{\mathrm{rot}} is sign-free (i.e., positive-definite), by the Perron–Frobenius theorem.

Although the MSR is exact only in the unfrustrated case, it remains a remarkably accurate approximation for the sign structure of the ground state wavefunction up to moderate frustration (J2≲0.5J_{2}\lesssim 0.5), as confirmed by exact diagonalization (ED) studies [51]. In our work, we explicitly encode this sign structure into the Hamiltonians used for variational learning. Additionally, for both the AHM and J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model we carry out all simulations in the zero total-magnetization sector of the Hilbert space.

V Training Algorithms and Hyperparameters

In this section we discuss the training algorithms and hyperparameters used to train SineKAN architectures for the transverse field Ising model (TFIM) (section V.1), anisotropic Heisenberg model (AHM) (section VI) and the J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model (section VI.1). We consider the chain length L=20L=20 for TFIM, AHM, and for the J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model, we study the chain lengths L=20,32,64L=20,32,64 and 100100.

V.1 TFIM

For all the computations of the TFIM, the spins are sampled with the MetropolisLocal algorithm. The sampler is configured with 1024 parallel Markov chains, and the number of samples and the chunk size are also set to 1024, ensuring that sampling is fully parallelized with no internal batching. A fixed random seed is used to ensure reproducibility. Both models used three SineKAN layers with a grid size of 8 and hidden layer dimensions (64, 64). The wave function is optimized using the Adam optimizer, with a linearly decaying learning rate schedule defined via optax. Specifically, the learning rate starts at 10−410^{-4} for the first 5,000 training epochs and decays linearly to 10−610^{-6} over the remaining 5,000 epochs. This schedule allows for rapid initial convergence while ensuring stable updates in the later stages of optimization. For the zero–transverse‐field Ising point, we instead use the learning rate of 10−210^{-2} to avoid strong local minima and for 100 iterations since the ground state rapidly converges for this point.

VI AHM

All sampling, ansatz, and optimizer settings are identical to those in Sec. V.1. However, in the gapped phase as γ→1\gamma\to 1, the spectral gap between the GS and the 1st1^{\mathrm{st}} excited state decreases continuously and becomes vanishingly small by γ≈0.6\gamma\approx 0.6 as shown in fig. 2. Consequently, SineKAN with MetropolisLocal sampling becomes inefficient and gets trapped in a local minimum, leading to incorrect GS energies. We overcome this difficulty by adopting a Zeeman bias [52]. For 0<γ<0.90<\gamma<0.9, we augment H⁡(h)=Hγ−h​∑iS^izH(h)=H_{\gamma}-h\sum_{i}\hat{S}^{z}_{i} while for γ≥0.9\gamma\geq 0.9 (the Ising limit) we instead use H⁡(h)=Hγ−h​∑iS^ixH(h)=H_{\gamma}-h\sum_{i}\hat{S}^{x}_{i}. This bias lifts the Néel degeneracy by an energy ∝L​h\propto Lh and yields a unique nondegenerate GS.

The quench proceeds in two phases. First, we set the initial pinning strength to hinit=γ+0.2h_{\mathrm{init}}=\gamma+0.2. We then linearly ramp this field to zero in 15 equal steps: at each annealing stage n=0,⋯,14n=0,\cdots,14 we set hn=hinit​(1−n+115)h_{n}=h_{\mathrm{init}}\Bigl(1-\frac{n+1}{15}\Bigr) and perform 333 VMC iterations under the Hamiltonian H⁡(hn)H(h_{n}), for a total of 4995 iterations. Once the field reaches h=0h=0, we run an additional 5005 iterations on the bare Hamiltonian HγH_{\gamma} to finalize the wavefunction in the true zero-field GS. For γ\gamma between −1-1 to 00 no pinning or bias was applied.

VI.1 J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} Model

All SineKAN architectires are trained using the Adam optimizer [53]. They are also trained with the same schedule of 30K epochs at a fixed learning rate followed by a decay down to 0.2 times the initial learning rate over 4K epochs. The learning rates for each model were found empirically by checking learning rates from 1×10−21\times 10^{-2} to 1×10−61\times 10^{-6} and the associated performance in evaluating GS energy values compared to DMRG. For SineKAN the learning rate was found to be 1×10−31\times 10^{-3} for values of J2<0.3J_{2}<0.3 and 1×10−41\times 10^{-4} for values of J2≥0.3J_{2}\geq 0.3, for MLP it was found to be 1×10−31\times 10^{-3} for J2<0.4J_{2}<0.4 and 1×10−41\times 10^{-4} for J2≥0.4J_{2}\geq 0.4, for RNN-LSTM it was found to be 1×10−31\times 10^{-3}, and for RBM it was found to be 1×10−51\times 10^{-5}.

The models are fitted using the NetKet [54] library with 1024 samples. For the RBM and SineKAN models, the local Metropolis-Hastings algorithm was used while for the autoregressive direct sampler algorithm designed for use with the NetKet RNN-LSTM model was used.

The vSineKAN and rSineKAN models were constructed from three SineKAN layers with a grid size of 8 and output dimensions of 64, 64, and 1. The vMLP and rMLP models were constructed from three linear layers with output dimensions of 256, 256, and 1 with ReLU functions following the first two hidden layers [43].

The RNN-LSTM model was constructed with three hidden layers each with a hidden dimension of 64. The RBM was constructed with an alpha value (number of connections per feature) of 128. A table of model parameter numbers for lattice of size L=100L=100 can be found in table 1.

For reasons explained in section X, and as shown in table 2, a grid size of 7 is used rather than 8 for L=64L=64.

All models were trained on a single T4 GPU with 16GB of VRAM.

VII Results

VII.1 TFIM

We begin by benchmarking the vSineKAN and the rSineKAN on the L=20L=20 transverse field Ising chain. For transverse field values h∈[0.0,1.6]h\in[0.0,1.6], we compute the GS energy, energy variance σ2≡⟨H^2⟩−⟨H^⟩2\sigma^{2}\equiv\langle\hat{H}^{2}\rangle-\langle\hat{H}\rangle^{2}, and the spin-spin correlation function defined as m2​(h)=1L​∑i⟨σ^iz​σ^i+L/2z⟩hm^{2}(h)=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{i}\langle\hat{\sigma}^{z}_{i}\hat{\sigma}^{z}_{i+L/2}\rangle_{h} and compare the results with ED. The relative error in energy is given by

ϵED=|EED−EModel||EED|\epsilon_{\mathrm{ED}}=\frac{|E_{\mathrm{ED}}-E_{\mathrm{Model}}|}{|E_{\mathrm{ED}}|} (11)

In fig. 3, we plot the energy error and variance, as well as the spin-spin correlation m2​(h)m^{2}(h), as functions of the transverse field hh.

As shown in fig. 3, both vSineKAN and rSineKAN ansatz performs extremely well, achieving high energy accuracy and wave function quality, as indicated by the lower values of ϵED\epsilon_{\mathrm{ED}} and σ2\sigma^{2} across the entire range of hh. The spin-spin correlation m2​(h)m^{2}(h) closely follows the ED results for both ansatz, with the symmetric model providing slightly better agreement near the critical point hc≈1h_{c}\approx 1.

VII.2 AHM

In the second benchmark of our ansatz, we compute the GS energy, variance and fidelity of the AHM HγH_{\gamma} for γ∈[−1,1]\gamma\in[-1,1] and compare the GS energy with ED results for a chain of length L=20L=20. In fig. 4, we plot the relative energy error, variance and fidelity for different values of anisotropy. For −1≤γ≤0-1\leq\gamma\leq 0 (no Zeeman bias), both the SineKAN ansatz maintain εED<5×10−4\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ED}}<5\times 10^{-4}.

For 0<γ≤10<\gamma\leq 1, where a Zeeman bias is applied, the near-critical window 0.1≤γ≤0.40.1\leq\gamma\leq 0.4 produces the largest deviations: the vSineKAN error peaks at εED​(0.3)≈3.2×10−3\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ED}}(0.3)\approx 3.2\times 10^{-3} while the rSineKAN remains below εED​(0.4)≈1.4×10−3\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ED}}(0.4)\approx 1.4\times 10^{-3}. As the bias reopens the gap for γ≳0.6\gamma\gtrsim 0.6, both ansatz recover εED<10−4\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ED}}<10^{-4}, and by γ≥0.9\gamma\geq 0.9 both errors fall below 10−510^{-5}, vanishing at γ=1\gamma=1.

The fidelity FF between the exact GS and the SineKAN variational wavefunction is defined as:

F=|⟨ψED|ψSineKAN⟩|2⟨ψED|ψED⟩​⟨ψSineKAN|ψSineKAN⟩.F=\frac{|\langle\psi_{\text{ED}}|\psi_{\text{SineKAN}}\rangle|^{2}}{\langle\psi_{\text{ED}}|\psi_{\text{ED}}\rangle\langle\psi_{\text{SineKAN}}|\psi_{\text{SineKAN}}\rangle}. (12)

As shown in the fig. 4, in the unbiased range −1≤γ≤0-1\leq\gamma\leq 0, both model achieve F>0.99F>0.99 (e.g. Fr​(−1)=0.99997F_{r}(-1)=0.99997, Fv​(−1)=0.99992F_{v}(-1)=0.99992, and at γ=0\gamma=0, Fr=0.99916F_{r}=0.99916, Fv=0.99833F_{v}=0.99833). In the biased region 0<γ<10<\gamma<1, however, the vSineKAN partially fails to lift the Néel degeneracy despite quenching and its fidelity collapses to approximately 0.500.50 for 0.5≤γ≤0.90.5\leq\gamma\leq 0.9. By contrast, the symmetric model maintains F>0.99F>0.99 everywhere (e.g. Fr​(0.6)≈0.996F_{r}(0.6)\approx 0.996, Fr​(0.8)≈0.995F_{r}(0.8)\approx 0.995). At γ=1\gamma=1 both fidelities recover to unity.

As shown in the figure fig. 4, both ansatz maintain σ2<10−2\sigma^{2}<10^{-2}, but the rSineKAN keeps σ2<10−3\sigma^{2}<10^{-3} throughout, yielding an order‐of‐magnitude reduction in statistical fluctuations.

VII.3 Benchmark of J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} Model Against ED

In the third benchmark, we assess the accuracy of SineKAN in describing the GS of the 1D J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model through a comprehensive set of numerical test for system size L=20L=20. We evaluate the GS energy, the fidelity between ED and SineKAN GS wavefunction, as well as compute isotropic spin–spin and dimer–dimer correlation functions, and structure factors, comparing the results directly against ED. These comparisons test the ability of the SineKAN to faithfully represent not only the GS energy but also nontrivial correlation properties of the wavefunction for the frustrated spin system.

We begin by evaluating the GS energy and fidelity between variational wavefunctions corresponding to different values of J2=0.0J_{2}=0.0 to 0.60.6, using both the vSineKAN and rSineKAN ansatz. For the special case at the MG point at J2=0.5J_{2}=0.5, there is a two-fold degeneracy of the GS with identical energy of −7.5-7.5. The fidelity at this point is then calculated as the sum of the fidelity with each of the two orthonormal GS eigenvectors.

As shown in fig. 5, the rSineKAN model exhibits excellent fidelity with the exact GS across the unfrustrated and moderately frustrated regimes, specifically for 0≤J2≤0.50\leq J_{2}\leq 0.5. In this range, the GS fidelity remains very close to unity, indicating that the ansatz successfully captures the essential features of the GS wavefunction.

As shown in table 3, for the case of J2=0.4J_{2}=0.4, the system is gapped, with a very small energy difference between the GS and the 1st1^{\mathrm{st}} excited state. The vSineKAN model at this point shows a high fidelity (∼0.799\sim 0.799) with the GS and a fidelity of ∼0.192\sim 0.192 with the 1st1^{\mathrm{st}} excited state with almost no contribution from higher excited states. Due to the small energy gap between the GS and 1st1^{\mathrm{st}} excited state, the GS energy of vSineKAN of −7.598-7.598 represents an overlap between the two lowest energy states. rSineKAN, however, is able reach a fidelity of ∼1\sim 1 with the GS as seen in fig. 5.

The vSineKAN also performs well in the unfrustrated regime and retains high fidelity with the exact GS for J2≤0.3J_{2}\leq 0.3. In this region, the ansatz is sufficiently expressive to capture the GS properties accurately.

Interestingly, in the highly frustrated regime at J2=0.6J_{2}=0.6, both the vSineKAN and rSineKAN exhibit a sharp drop in fidelity, with values around ∼0.40%\sim 0.40\%. This significant decline indicates that neither of our ansatz is able to faithfully represent the true GS in this regime. The poor performance can be attributed to the violation of the MSR, which is no longer satisfied J2>0.5J_{2}>0.5. In fact, the fidelity itself serves as a useful diagnostic tool to quantify the extent to which MSR is violated. A qualitative analysis of this case and its connection to MSR breakdown is presented in section VIII. Since the rSineKAN achieves higher fidelity compared to the vSineKAN, we use the former throughout the rest of the section.

The spin-spin correlation functions are defined as

Cγ​γ​(r)=1L​∑ℓ=1L⟨S^ℓγ​S^ℓ+rγ⟩C^{\gamma\gamma}(r)=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\langle\hat{S}_{\ell}^{\gamma}\hat{S}_{\ell+r}^{\gamma}\rangle (13)

where, ⟨⋯⟩\langle\cdots\rangle represents the expectation value taken over the variational wavefunction and γ≡x,y\gamma\equiv x,y or zz. Following [16], we compute the isotropic spin-spin correlations C⁡(r)=13​(Cx​x+Cy​y+Cz​z)C(r)=\frac{1}{3}(C^{xx}+C^{yy}+C^{zz}), for J2=0J_{2}=0, using rSineKAN and compare its result against the ED for a system of L=20L=20. As shown in the fig. 6, the rSineKAN reproduces ED results with high accuracy across all distances.

For J2>J2cJ_{2}>J_{2}^{c}, the system becomes gapped, with a dimerized two-fold degenerate GS that breaks translational invariance [55]. The emergence of this dimer order can be probed using the connected dimer–dimer correlation function: [16]

D⁡(r)=1L​∑ℓ=1L⟨S^ℓz​S^ℓ+1z​S^ℓ+rz​S^ℓ+r+1z⟩−[Cz​z​(r=1)]2D(r)=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\langle\hat{S}^{z}_{\ell}\hat{S}^{z}_{\ell+1}\hat{S}^{z}_{\ell+r}\hat{S}^{z}_{\ell+r+1}\rangle-[C^{zz}(r=1)]^{2} (14)

where, Cz​z​(r=1)=1L​∑ℓ=1LS^ℓz​S^ℓ+1zC^{zz}(r=1)=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\hat{S}^{z}_{\ell}\hat{S}^{z}_{\ell+1}. For rSineKAN and ED, the plot of D⁡(r)D(r) as a function rr for J2=0,0.4,0.5J_{2}=0,0.4,0.5 and 0.60.6 with system size L=20L=20 are shown in fig. 7. There is a strong agreement in D⁡(r)D(r) between the ED solution and rSineKAN for J2≤0.5J_{2}\leq 0.5. The overall pattern is still preserved at J2=0.6J_{2}=0.6 but the correlation values start to diverge from ED.

The spin structure factor [1] is defined as

S⁡(k)=1L​∑i,j=1Lei⁡(i−j)​k​⟨S^iz​S^jz⟩S(k)=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{i,j=1}^{L}e^{i(i-j)k}\langle\hat{S}^{z}_{i}\hat{S}^{z}_{j}\rangle (15)

In the regime J2≪J1J_{2}\ll J_{1}, strong quantum fluctuations prevent the system from developing true long-range order, which is reflected in a divergence of S⁡(k)S(k) at k=πk=\pi. For the range J2c<J2<0.5J_{2}^{c}<J_{2}<0.5, spin fluctuations remain commensurate, meaning the peak of S⁡(k)S(k) stays at k=πk=\pi. At the MG point, J2=0.5J_{2}=0.5, the system becomes dimerized and gapped, while still maintaining the peak of S⁡(k)S(k) at k=πk=\pi. fig. 8 shows the plots of S⁡(k)S(k) versus kk for J2=0,0.4J_{2}=0,0.4 and 0.50.5, obtained using both rSineKAN and ED.

VII.4 Benchmarking J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} Model for L=32,64L=32,64, & 100100

We compute the relative error of the SineKAN GS energy with respect to the DMRG result for system sizes L=32,64L=32,64 and 100100 as:

ϵDMRG≡|EDMRG−ESineKAN||EDMRG|\epsilon_{\mathrm{DMRG}}\equiv\frac{|E_{\mathrm{DMRG}}-E_{\mathrm{SineKAN}}|}{|E_{\mathrm{DMRG}}|} (16)

and the variance σ2\sigma^{2} computed over a sample of configurations.

We compare the performance of rSineKAN and vSineKAN in terms of relative error (fig. 9) and variance (fig. 10). We find that for smaller lattices of size L=32L=32 and L=64L=64, there is generally not a large substantial difference between rSineKAN and vSineKAN. However, for L=100L=100, the addition of reflection symmetry in rSineKAN leads to a significant improvement in relative error and variance. The approximate magnitude of relative error is one to three orders of magnitude less for rSineKAN compared to vSineKAN for L=100L=100 and J2<0.6J_{2}<0.6 and the variance is approximately zero to five orders of magnitude less.

For rSineKAN with size L=100L=100, at J2=0.0,0.4J_{2}=0.0,0.4 and 0.50.5 the percentage errors (100×ϵDMRG100\times\epsilon_{\mathrm{DMRG}}) are of the order of ∼0.03%\sim 0.03\%, ∼0.04%\sim 0.04\% and ∼0.001%\sim 0.001\% respectively. The most significant improvement is at the MG point. At this point, the GS corresponds to exact VBS order. This means, since knowing one spin of each pair gives the other spin, the effective parameter space is reduced from 2L2^{L} to 2L/22^{L/2}. rSineKAN is more able to effectively model this point.

We also directly compared, for L=100L=100, the performance of the RBM, RNN-LSTM, vSineKAN, rSineKAN, vMLP, and rMLP ansätze for J2=0.0−0.6J_{2}=0.0-0.6. A comprehensive summary of findings of comparison of the rSineKAN and vSineKAN ansätze to RBM and RNN-LSTM can be found in fig. 11. Here we see that rSineKAN outperforms the other ansätze across the board on approximation of the DMRG GS energy and low variance with the sole exception of best variance for RNN-LSTM on J2=0.3J_{2}=0.3. We see the comparison of rSineKAN and vSineKAN to vMLP and rMLP in fig. 11. Here we see that rSineKAN outperforms an MLP with similar number of parameters. The inclusion of reflection symmetry leads to an improvement of the result for both MLP and SineKAN but with the best overall result corresponding to rSineKAN.

Previous work has used translationally invariant transformers to study the L=100L=100 J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} spin chain [16]. They found an approximate value of ϵ\epsilon ϵDMRG\epsilon_{\mathrm{DMRG}} of 1.65×10−4~1.65\times 10^{-4} for J2=0.4J_{2}=0.4 and 7.36×10−6~7.36\times 10^{-6} for J2=0.0J_{2}=0.0. The errors for rSineKAN were 4.64×10−44.64\times 10^{-4} for J2=0.4J_{2}=0.4 and 2.96×10−42.96\times 10^{-4} for J2=0.0J_{2}=0.0 respectively.

VIII MSR in SineKAN

It is known that the MSR holds exactly at J2=0J_{2}=0 and remain approximately valid for 0<J2≤0.50<J_{2}\leq 0.5 in the 1D J1​–​J2J_{1}\text{--}J_{2} model; however, the sign structure of the GS becomes non-trivial for J2>0.5J_{2}>0.5 [51, 56]. There are three different ways of incorporating MSR into NQS architectures. One approach is to train the model without any prior encoding of MSR, allowing it to learn the sign structure over the course of optimization [16]. Another strategy involves using two separate NNs: one to represent the amplitude and another to learn the phase of the variational wave function, without explicitly enforcing MSR [57]. A third method is to implement MSR at the Hamiltonian level together with a predefined, fixed phase structure embedded directly into the ansatz [10].

In our model, we incorporated the MSR in the Hamiltonian without introducing any additional phase structure in the variational wave function. To determine how well our ansatz captures the sign structure we plotted the ϵDMRG\epsilon_{\mathrm{DMRG}} as a function of J2J_{2} for L=32,64,100L=32,64,100, as shown in (fig. 12). For J2≤0.5J_{2}\leq 0.5, the error ϵDMRG\epsilon_{\mathrm{DMRG}} remains consistently small across all system sizes, indicating that the MSR is well respected in this regime. This suggests that our ansatz accurately captures the GS sign structure without requiring any additional phase learning.

In the highly frustrated regime at J2=0.6J_{2}=0.6 for the system sizes of L=32,64,100L=32,64,100, the GS energy computed by rSineKAN has a percentage error approximately 1.3%1.3\% from the corresponding DMRG values, indicating that rSineKAN struggles to accurately capture the sign structure in this region. For L=20L=20, the fidelity between the rSineKAN and the exact GS wavefunction decreases from ∼100%\sim 100\% at J2<0.6J_{2}<0.6 to approximately ∼41%\sim 41\% at J2=0.6J_{2}=0.6. Additionally, the error (ϵDMRG\epsilon_{\mathrm{DMRG}}) is roughly the same ∼1.3%\sim 1.3\% for L=32L=32, 6464, and 100100 as shown in fig. 12. The behavior of rSineKAN is consistent for J2=0.6J_{2}=0.6 across different lattice sizes, and we attribute this directly to violation of MSR for J2>0.5J_{2}>0.5 and not directly to any particular choice of the ansatz. This is supported by results shown in fig. 11 and fig. 12 where rSineKAN has the best estimation of the DMRG energy result among ansätze for J2=0.6J_{2}=0.6.

IX Inference Time

We compare inference times on a single forward pass with an input vector of size (1,L)(1,L) representing a single lattice of length LL. We plot inference time as a function of LL for L=16,32,64,128,256L=16,32,64,128,256. Results were averaged over 100,000 forward passes with each preceded by 200,000 warm up iterations to ensure consistent behavior on GPU. The GPU used was a single NVIDIA T4 GPU with 16GB of RAM. For the RBM we use 128 features per node, for RNN-LSTM we use three hidden layers each with 64 features, for vSineKAN and rSineKAN we use a grid size of 8 and layer sizes of (64,64,1)(64,64,1), and for vMLP and rMLP we use layer sizes of (256,256,1)(256,256,1). We see in fig. 13 which has log10\log_{10} y-axis and log2\log_{2} x-axis that SineKAN and MLP architectures show roughly flat scaling and only deviate significantly at L=256L=256 where the cost contribution from the first layer is large enough that linear scaling takes over. RNN-LSTM shows a linear growth in inference time and RBM, while fastest for small lattice sizes, shows an exponential growth in inference time. vMLP and rMLP have faster inference than vSineKAN and rSineKAN.

X Discussion

In this paper, we present the SineKAN model as a potential ansatz for NQS wavefunctions. The motivation to explore KAN architectures stems from the KAST [29, 30] and supporting literature on the effectiveness of various KAN ansatz [37]. The specific choice of SineKAN was inspired by its strong numerical performance in function approximation and scalability relative to other KAN variants [36]. Moreover, SineKAN has been shown to effectively generalize patterns beyond the training domain, further motivating its exploration [36].

In section VII we establish the efficacy of including reflection symmetry about the center of the lattice. Passing the input spins and the center-reflected input spins to the same multilayer SineKAN and then summing to make the combined rSineKAN effectively halves the total parameter space and stabilizes performance at minimal cost. We establish, using multiple benchmarks of GS energy, correlation functions, and structure factors, that the vSineKAN ansatz is numerically accurate for modeling L=20L=20 TFIM, AHM, and J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} systems and that these results can be improved further by adding a minimal reflection symmetry in rSineKAN. In particular, to resolve the near‐degeneracy of the two Néel product states for γ>0\gamma>0 in the AHM, we introduced a small Zeeman bias hinit=γ+0.2h_{\mathrm{init}}=\gamma+0.2 and annealed it to zero over the course of the VMC optimization. This bias lifts the twofold Néel degeneracy by an energy, selects a unique nondegenerate GS, and substantially improves convergence in the positive γ−\gamma-regime. For the case AHM, vSineKAN is unable to resolve the ground state and excited states from γ=0.5\gamma=0.5 to 0.90.9 due to the vanishing energy gap. However, rSineKAN is able to resolve the GS, likely due to the reflection symmetry reducing the total search space by a factor of two and stabilizing model behavior.

Furthermore, we show later in section VII that for J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} spin chain of L=100L=100, including reflection symmetry leads to an improvement in performance for both SineKAN and MLP-based architectures. It should be noted that the improvement in performance is more significant from vSineKAN to rSineKAN than for vMLP to rMLP. We also recommend that, for other lattice geometries, appropriate discrete symmetries be included. Given sufficient resources, this could even include computationally expensive symmetries such as translational invariance, which would require, as an upper limit, a number of forward passes equal to the lattice size.

In the section VII, we show that the model achieves substantially more accurate results in estimation of the GS energy at lower variance across configurations when compared to benchmark RNN-LSTM, MLP and RBM models. We also find that SineKAN is highly computationally efficient compared to RNN-LSTM with similar numbers of parameters and numerically competitive with MLP architectures with the same number of parameters and the same reflection symmetry. Based on these findings, we expect that rSineKAN ansatz will be highly competitive with other ansätze for NQS. A particular indicator of the efficacy of rSineKAN is that it is the only ansatz explored in this paper that is consistently able to model, with extremely low relative error and variance, the MG point in the J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model. This strongly motivates the choice of rSineKAN as an ansatz for NQS.

We also compare to previous results using translationally invariant vision transformers (ViT) [16]. It is difficult to directly compare these models due to differences in computational resources and algorithms used, however ViT outperforms rSineKAN for J2=0.0J_{2}=0.0 and 0.40.4. Due to the authors’ reported significantly increased sample size and the use of the stochastic reconfiguration algorithm, we estimate training these models would have required, at minimum, on the order of twice the amount of compute resources in both RAM and time. Future work might explore the use of full translational invariance in combination with SineKAN layers. Furthermore, SineKAN layers could potentially be used in heads in transformer architectures, possibly in place of MLP heads.

We incorporate the MSR into the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} Hamiltonian, which yields accurate results for rSineKAN in the regime J2=0J_{2}=0 to 0.50.5 for the chain length L=32,64L=32,64, and 100100. However, the violation of the MSR for J2=0.6J_{2}=0.6, results in a noticeable drop in performance. In this regime, all other ansatz also perform poorly, with the best result still coming from rSineKAN, which maintains a consistent relative error with respect to DMRG, ϵDMRG∼1.3%\epsilon_{\mathrm{DMRG}}\sim 1.3\%, independent of the chain length.

There exists an anomalous case for SineKAN. Due to symmetries in the phase shifts in SineKAN, when hidden layer dimension is sufficiently similar to LL and, simultaneously, the grid size is equal to L\sqrt{L}, predictive performance of the models becomes substantially worse. This can be clearly seen in table 2. To account for this, we use a grid size of 7 rather than 8 for L=64L=64. This is generally easily predictable and avoidable for cases where the layer sizes match the input dimension nearly exactly and simply require adjusting the grid size to be at least N±1\sqrt{N}\pm 1 and not exactly N\sqrt{N}. We show that changing the grid size by one resolves this issue. We posit that this is likely related to specific alignments of the grid and input phase shifts but further exploration is needed to confirm this.

We also show the computational scaling for SineKAN architectures compared to other ansätze. SineKAN has scaling much more comparable to the highly efficient MLP architectures, while RNN-LSTM has larger polynomial scaling and RBM has exponential scaling. Additionally, the rSineKAN model is highly accurate even when using 10241024 samples in the configuration and sampling over 34K iterations. This represents only ∼3.5×107\sim 3.5\times 10^{7} total spin configurations sampled from the total parameter space of 2100≈1.3×10302^{100}\approx 1.3\times 10^{30}. It’s likely that increasing the configuration size and model parameters in future longer training runs on high-performance computing systems could lead to more accurate results.

Beyond the benchmark applications explored in this work, the SineKAN architecture holds promise for a wide range of quantum many-body systems. Its flexibility and expressivity make it a compelling candidate for studying critical phenomena in 1D quantum materials. Future work could include applications in ferromagnetic spin chains, magnetic polymer chains and aggregates [58, 59, 60], and magnetic atomic chains—systems where entanglement features and nontrivial correlations play a pivotal role. Moreover, the model may offer valuable insights into avalanche-like magnetization dynamics in artificial spin ices, where nanomagnets are arranged on tailored lattices. The rSineKAN ansatz could also be extended to incorporate many-body interactions relevant to fermionic and bosonic systems, potentially extending its applicability to more complex condensed matter settings.

XI Conclusion & Outlook

In this paper we introduce SineKAN as a potential ansatz for the NQS approach for describing the GS of quantum many-body systems. We show strong empirical evidence that the model has a high degree of accuracy with low variance in computing GS energies and correlation functions of TFIM, AHM, and J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} systems when compared to ED for a lattice size of L=20L=20. We further show that, for lattice sizes of L=32,64L=32,64, and 100100, SineKAN models are highly accurate compared to the results from the DMRG algorithm. Changing only the input chain length, LL, in the first layer of SineKAN, robust numerical results can be achieved with a linear increase in the model size as a function of LL.

We benchmark SineKAN against MLP, RBM and RNN-LSTM models for a lattice size of L=100L=100. The best performing model was found to be rSineKAN which adds a reflection symmetry about the center with low computation cost increase. We find that the rSineKAN model outperformed the RNN-LSTM ansatz despite RNN-LSTM including both short and long distance relationships across the lattice and rSineKAN using a fraction of the total computation cost. We also compare with MLP architectures with a slightly larger number of parameters and found that rSineKAN still significantly outperforms rMLP both in terms of low error and low variance meaning that the improvement in performance cannot be solely attributed to including reflection symmetry. We also benchmark against RBM which is a commonly used benchmark ansatz for NQS due to physics motivations of RBM having an Ising model structure. We find that rSineKAN significantly outperforms a RBM with a substantially larger number of parameters.

We show empirically that SineKAN is a promising ansatz which is worth exploring for future work on NQS. The models trained in this work can all be trained in less than 24 hours on a single Nvidia T4 GPU and can be run offline for inference on a laptop using only a CPU and 16GB of RAM. We have strong reason to believe that significant improvements can be achieved using greater computational resources. Further exploration might include larger configuration sizes, larger models, and additional symmetries, as well as generalizations of these approaches to other lattice geometries.

A key motivation for exploring KAN-based NQS was to investigate whether incorporating the KAST structure leads to improved approximations of the GS energy in the highly frustrated regime. While our results show clear improvements over traditional architectures such as RBM in the large J2J_{2} region, the model can still become trapped in local minima. A possible future direction is to extend the SineKAN frequencies and amplitudes into the complex domain, a technique which has been shown in other works to lead to improvement in learning the sign structure of models in the highly frustrated regime [16, 51].

Appendix A Variational Monte Carlo

Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) [2] is a powerful method for approximating the GS of a quantum system. It works in two steps. First, the quantum expectation value of the energy is cast into a classical Monte Carlo sampling problem over a probability distribution defined by a trial wavefunction that depends on a set of variational parameters. Second, the parameters of this wavefunction are optimized to minimize the estimated energy using stochastic optimization techniques.

For a trial wavefunction written in the computational basis as Ψθ=∑σψθ​(σ)​|σ⟩\Psi_{\theta}=\sum_{\sigma}\psi_{\theta}(\sigma)\ket{\sigma}, which depends on a set of variational parameters θ\theta, the energy expectation value is given by

Eθ=⟨Ψθ|​H​|Ψθ⟩⟨Ψθ|Ψθ⟩≥E0.E_{\theta}=\frac{\bra{\Psi_{\theta}}H\ket{\Psi_{\theta}}}{\braket{\Psi_{\theta}|\Psi_{\theta}}}\geq E_{0}. (17)

where E0E_{0} the exact GS energy serving as the lower bound. Inserting a resolution of identity in the computational basis and defining ψθ​(σ)=⟨σ|ψθ⟩\psi_{\theta}(\sigma)=\braket{\sigma|\psi_{\theta}}, the energy expectation can be expressed as

Eθ=∑σpθ​(σ)​Eloc​(σ|θ)=⟨⟨Eloc​(σ|θ)⟩⟩,E_{\theta}=\sum_{\sigma}p_{\theta}(\sigma)E_{\mathrm{loc}}(\sigma|\theta)=\langle\langle E_{\mathrm{loc}}(\sigma|\theta)\rangle\rangle, (18)

with ⟨⟨⋯⟩⟩\langle\langle\cdots\rangle\rangle denoting the expectation value with respect to the pθ​(σ)p_{\theta}(\sigma). Here the local energy is given by

Eloc​(σ|θ)=∑σ′⟨σ′|​H​|σ⟩​ψθ​(σ′)ψθ​(σ),E_{\mathrm{loc}}(\sigma|\theta)=\sum_{\sigma^{\prime}}\bra{\sigma^{\prime}}H\ket{\sigma}\frac{\psi_{\theta}(\sigma^{\prime})}{\psi_{\theta}(\sigma)}, (19)

and is computed for each sampled configuration σ\sigma and the probability distribution is defined as

pθ​(σ)=|ψθ​(σ)|2/∑σ|ψθ​(σ)|2p_{\theta}(\sigma)=|\psi_{\theta}(\sigma)|^{2}/\sum_{\sigma}|\psi_{\theta}(\sigma)|^{2} (20)

For any observable, then, we can always compute expectation values over arbitrary wave functions as a statistical average. The great majority of physical observables, and for a given σ\sigma, the number of elements σ′\sigma^{\prime} connected by those matrix elements is polynomial in the system size; thus, the summation in local energy can be carried out systematically. The essential idea of the VMC is, therefore, to replace these sums over exponentially many states, with a statistical average over a large but finite set of states sampled according to the probability distribution pθ​(σ)p_{\theta}(\sigma).

Having introduced the Monte Carlo procedure for estimating the energy in large systems, the next step is to optimize the variational parameters. It is straightforward to show that the gradient of the energy can also be written under the form of the expectation value of some stochastic variable. In particular, define

Dk​(σ)=1Ψθ​(σ)​∂∂θk​Ψθ​(σ)=∂∂θk​log⁡Ψθ​(σ)D_{k}(\sigma)=\frac{1}{\Psi_{\theta}(\sigma)}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_{k}}\Psi_{\theta}(\sigma)=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_{k}}\log\Psi_{\theta}(\sigma) (21)

the gradient of the energy expectation value with respect to the parameters 𝜽\bm{\theta} can be written as

∂∂θk​⟨⟨Eloc​(σ|θ)⟩⟩=⟨⟨Gk⟩⟩\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta_{k}}\langle\langle E_{\mathrm{loc}}(\sigma|\theta)\rangle\rangle=\langle\langle G_{k}\rangle\rangle (22)

with the statistical expectation value of the gradient estimator

Gk=⟨⟨2Re[Dk(σ)−⟨⟨Dk(σ)⟩⟩]Eloc(σ|θ)G_{k}=\langle\langle 2\mathrm{Re}[D_{k}(\sigma)-\langle\langle D_{k}(\sigma)\rangle\rangle]E_{\mathrm{loc}}(\sigma|\theta) (23)

The parameters can be iteratively updated using gradient descent until the energy converges.

In practice, the sampling of configurations σ\sigma is typically performed using the Metropolis–Hastings algorithm, which generates a Markov chain of spin configurations distributed according to the probability pθ​(σ)p_{\theta}(\sigma). Once a sufficiently large and equilibrated set of samples is collected, the gradient estimates can be computed. For the optimization step, simple stochastic gradient descent may be used, but more sophisticated techniques such as the stochastic reconfiguration (SR) [2, 64] method—also known as natural gradient descent—are often preferred. These take into account the underlying geometry of the variational manifold, leading to improved stability and convergence properties in high-dimensional parameter spaces.
